title: Will Skills Replace MCP? Exploring the Advantages and Future of MCP
content:
LLM translation

This article was translated from Chinese by an LLM with minimal human revision. Chinese version

Absurd! The Fallacy That Skills Will Replace MCP

Since Agent Skills appeared and strongly promoted the idea that it saves tokens through progressive disclosure, discussion of MCP has dropped sharply across social media. Claims like “Skills are better than MCP” and “Skills will replace MCP” have popped up everywhere.

I’ve noticed that most software engineers use MCP or Skills as end users without trying to understand the differences and the underlying principles. As engineers, we shouldn’t adopt a technology just because it’s popular or because a big company engineer, a hot AI startup, or a tech influencer says so. We should think for ourselves.

So this post is a short summary of my current thoughts on MCP’s development, and why Skills cannot replace MCP. It is also intended to give developers some points to consider when choosing between Skills or MCP.

Why Progressive Disclosure Shouldn’t Be a Skill-Only Privilege

At first, Skills rose to fame by claiming “token savings”, and within days it became a hot topic among community coders. So what is the secret behind Skills being more token-efficient than the MCP servers people knew at the time?

Progressive Disclosure

Anthropic introduced the concept of progressive disclosure, a way to fetch information step by step so you don’t waste tokens by loading a large amount of irrelevant data all at once.

This article is not a primer on Skills or progressive disclosure, so I won’t dive deeply into the mechanics here. In short, Skills split information into three levels:

  1. Metadata / Index
  2. Instructions / Details
  3. Resources and code / Deep Dive
References
  • three levels of loading
  • What is Progressive Disclosure?
  • Progressive disclosure

In the metadata layer, the content in the SKILL.md frontmatter, only a small amount of information is stored, such as the skill name and a short description to let the agent know the skill’s purpose.

If the agent wants to use the skill or needs more confirmation, it reads the Instructions section, which is the SKILL.md body content.

Only when the skill really needs a particular asset does it read or use resources under scripts/, references/, or assets/.

This multi-step information retrieval avoids loading everything at once and wasting tokens on content that may never be needed.

Can MCP Implement Progressive Disclosure?

Once you understand progressive disclosure, the obvious question becomes: “if Skills can do it, can MCP do it too?”

Before discussing MCP, we need to clarify where progressive disclosure happens and who controls it. The conclusion is that these steps happen on the client side. In more familiar terms, this is like an LLM agent such as Gemini CLI, Claude Code, or OpenClaw.

These clients / agents execute the multi-stage retrieval process when they decide to use Skills. I won’t discuss client implementation details here, interested readers can refer to these examples.

So if progressive disclosure is a client-side behavior controlled by the client, then the technical answer to whether MCP can do it is clearly yes.

A simple example:

(If you are not familiar with the MCP spec yet, see MCP Specification)

In the original flow, the client uses tools/list to obtain all tool metadata, including descriptions, input schemas, and so on. The client uses that information to decide how to use the tools, then sends the chosen tool’s input. Readers who want the full flow can see Message Flow or the diagram below.

The most token-heavy step for the MCP server is the initial tools/list request. Suppose we have a self-built MCP server and a self-built client. Can we modify the current flow to achieve progressive disclosure?

txt
Original tool description:
  This is a tool for xxx, how to use...

New tool description:
  1. short description: This is a tool for xxx
  2. full description: how to use...

As shown above, we can split each tool description into two parts. One part becomes the short description, like the Skill frontmatter description, and the second part becomes the full description, like the Skill body content.

We can put the short description into the MCP Prompts description, and return the full description in the prompts/get response.

That means when the client sends a prompts/list request, the response contains only each tool’s short description. To understand how to use a tool, the client then sends prompts/get to receive the full usage details. By fetching information in layers, the client can finally execute tools/call for the desired tool.

Besides the approach I sketched using MCP prompts, there are other ways to support progressive disclosure without changing the current MCP spec, such as providing a dedicated tool to get short / full descriptions for other tools.

I won’t go deep into implementation details here because, in practice, changing the flow to support progressive disclosure has limitations. Popular MCP frameworks may not support it, and clients using that MCP server would need to follow the new message flow.

So my point is only to show that MCP can support progressive disclosure, and to prove that progressive disclosure or the so-called “token savings“ is not something Skills uniquely provide. This is not necessarily a recommendation for using this exact method in production or in client integration.

Beyond Token Savings: What Advantages Do Skills Actually Have?

This article is mainly about MCP, so I won’t spend too much time on Skills. But after the above argument, readers who originally only thought Skills were better because they saved tokens may still wonder: “Skills became popular for a reason, right?”

Here are a few advantages I think Skills bring:

  • Easy to customize for specific needs
    • Whether you write your own Skill or modify a downloaded one, most of the time you only need to edit text files.
  • Easy to produce
    • Related to the previous point, Skills are easy enough to create that users can let an agent like OpenClaw help write or record common requirements. Generating new Skills might not even need human intervention.
  • Transparent and easy to inspect
    • Unlike MCP, Skills content and execution logic can often be opened and viewed locally. It feels more like building an open source project yourself rather than running someone else’s binary.

MCP’s Path to Survival in the Skills Era

After discussing progressive disclosure and Skill advantages, we can return to what MCP offers that Skills cannot replace.

Most MCP vs Skills debates ignore remote MCP servers (or assume only local MCP servers are involved).

Remote vs Local

This article uses a very rough distinction between remote MCP servers and local MCP servers. A remote MCP server is one that is not installed on your own computer, connecting to a server hosted elsewhere counts as remote. A local MCP server runs on the same machine as the client, such as when you download someone else’s MCP server binary and run it locally alongside your agent.

Remote MCP Server

Comparing a remote server to local Skills may feel unfair for readers familiar with remote / local differences, but for those who are not, it is worth clarifying what remote MCP servers can do well:

  • Tools update without reinstalling
    • When a remote MCP server updates a tool, the client automatically uses the new version the next time it calls that tool.
  • Decide which tools a user can see and use based on identity, location, or other information
    • At tools/list time, the server can only show the tools the user is allowed to access. Tools that should not be available never appear, reducing the risk of token waste from choosing the wrong tool.
  • Centralize resource management
    • Resources can be managed centrally. For example, if some tools should only be used by X users at once, the server can decide whether to grant access.

These remote server advantages are similar to the benefits offered by traditional API servers. Almost any feature supported by an API gateway can be used in a remote MCP server, and readers can think through the trade-offs themselves.

Local MCP Server vs Skills?

After discussing what powerful remote servers can do, some may still think, “Those benefits are remote-only. So local MCP servers can be replaced by Skills, right?” Not necessarily.

Before MCP – LSP

Before MCP existed, there was already something in the field called the Language Server Protocol (LSP), which had been quietly working for years. LSP may not be glamorous, but it has played a critical role.

Many readers have installed extensions in VS Code. Some extensions related to programming languages make editing C++, Python, and so on much smoother. This is thanks to LSP, which defines a protocol that allows VS Code and other tools to request formatting, autocomplete, and more.

With LSP, client-side editor developers don’t need to build custom support for each language. Instead, language providers can implement extensions that offer functionality for their language. This saves time for client developers, keeps products focused, and gives users flexibility to choose the tools they need.

In the MCP spec Overview, it even says:

  • MCP takes some inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which standardizes how to add support for programming languages across a whole ecosystem of development tools. In a similar way, MCP standardizes how to integrate additional context and tools into the ecosystem of AI applications.

MCP and LSP are essentially trying to solve the same type of problem: how can a finished client (such as a development tool like VS Code or an AI application like Claude Code) obtain new capabilities from other developers through a well-defined protocol and workflow?

I mention LSP so readers understand that MCP is fundamentally a protocol, and that it is addressing a different problem space than Skills. This distinction is important for later discussion.

Local MCP Server

For a local MCP server, you can download a server binary and run it on your machine like an extension. The client sends requests to localhost:port.

The flexibility of MCP as a protocol is clear: the client only needs to know which tools are available and which one to call. The MCP server handles the rest.

The MCP server must manage tool execution, environment issues, permissions, and which programming language the tools are implemented in. As long as the server developer ensures the server can install and run on your machine, the client only needs basic MCP message flow support.

TIP

Most of the advantages discussed in this section apply equally to remote MCP servers.

MCP Tools vs Skills Scripts

Take Google’s Python Agent Development Kit (ADK) as an example. It is a framework for building agents, and it highlights a difficulty that arises when integrating Skills.

If the Skills you want to use are just markdown prompts, that is not a huge problem. But if a Skill also includes executable files in scripts/, the client now has to figure out how to run those files. They might be Python scripts or executable binaries, which is already the current common practice. But what if the script is C++, Java, or TypeScript? Many mainstream agents may not support that. Even with Python, dependencies and environment issues still need to be handled. Running the code in a container, VM, or on the host machine all differ, and dependencies need to be installed somewhere.

The Agent Skills spec itself says about scripts/:

  • Supported languages depend on the agent implementation. Common options include Python, Bash, and JavaScript.

In ADK, various code executors handle environment issues. At the time of writing, its execute_script_async function only supports .py, .sh, and .bash.

That means as a client developer, supporting Skills and supporting MCP require different levels of effort. If you want to solve all environment issues and give users a good Skills experience, it takes a lot of work. Supporting MCP only requires following the basic message flow.

Coroutine vs Process

I also want to mention a performance issue most people may not see. Using ADK’s unsafe_local_code_executor as an example, its execute_code function launches a separate process to run code.

If your agent usage is like a single-person interactive session with Gemini CLI or Claude Code, that is usually fine.

But if you are a developer building an agent as a backend service for many users, suppose someone exposes their OpenClaw server to the public, starting a new process for every Skill execution can quickly overwhelm the service. Converting the same Skill scripts into MCP tools and letting the MCP server handle requests with coroutines can reduce server load significantly.

Of course, actual design decisions depend on the scenario. I only want to highlight this as a point developers should be aware of.

Customizability Can Be a Double-Edged Sword

The fact that Skills are easy to modify is a big advantage. After downloading a Skill, users can adjust it for their needs. But that same modifiability can also be a weakness.

For example, if an LLM agent, or the LLM itself by mistake, edits someone else’s Skill, the Skill may behave unexpectedly the next time it runs. It could even be modified to include malicious behavior.

In contrast, modifying the execution logic of tools inside an MCP server is harder because the server binary is already packaged. Still, whether the downloaded MCP server is trustworthy is also something users must think about carefully.

How Should Developers Choose?

I’ll divide this into two perspectives: agent / client developers, and tool / Skill providers.

Agent (Client) Developers

For agent developers, using a framework like ADK is often unavoidable unless you have a large team and time to build your own agent from scratch. Frameworks usually provide some basic Skills support out of the box. MCP, on the other hand, may require no special work beyond connecting to an MCP server: if you can connect, you can use it.

Whether Skills need additional customization and support, such as browser automation or other fancy features, depends on what the developer team can build. If you are curious, see How to add skills support to your agent.

Tools / Skills Providers

For tools or Skills providers, assume you cannot modify the agent’s code, just like a VS Code extension developer cannot change VS Code itself. If a tool provider could change the agent code, they might as well implement the feature directly in the agent instead of using a protocol.

If you want to save time, be lazy, or let users customize solutions themselves, Skills can be a good choice. But if you care about performance, cross-language support, cross-platform compatibility, providing capabilities that clients may not support well with scripts, or minimizing client dependency, then MCP is often the better choice.

So far I have listed some pros, cons, and trade-offs. I don’t claim to have covered every angle. This article is meant as a starting point to help people think about the differences between the two.

The Future of MCP

We finally reach the end of the article! After so much discussion, do you still think Skills are clearly better and can replace MCP?

Take a look at SEP-2640: Skills Extension, a recent proposal for how to integrate Skills into MCP. Also follow the Skills Over MCP Working Group, the team driving this SEP.

Skills Over MCP Working Group experimental repo: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/experimental-ext-skills

Since everything is still under discussion, I won’t go into too many details here to avoid writing content that may soon become outdated.

In short, the current plan is to support Skills using MCP extensions, place Skill-related files in MCP Resources, and provide a new Common URI Schemes skill:// so clients can discover Skills.

With this approach, the progressive disclosure I mentioned at the beginning can be supported naturally by clients. The problem of needing both an MCP server and corresponding Skills to instruct an LLM agent would be solved: downloading one MCP server would give you both Skills and tools.

Conclusion

It has been a while since I wrote a blog post, and I chose a technical topic this time. Research alone took a lot of time, and even though the article is not long, finishing it took several hours.

What motivated me was the trend I’ve seen in recent years: fewer engineers seem willing to think deeply about technical details and trade-offs. It might also be lower visibility, creating the impression that people simply follow whatever is trending online.

I wrote this article to record my thoughts, help new readers distinguish between the two approaches, and show that technical details can evolve with the times. A new technology does not automatically replace an old one, and many capabilities are not unique to the newest option.

Do not appeal to authority.
